articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber-related and Transnational Criminal Organizations, Imposes New Cuba Sanctions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting cyber-related and transnational criminal organizations, alongside significant new sanctions against Cuba. OFAC designated four individuals and 41 entities linked to the Prince Group Transnational Criminal Organization (TCO), previously sanctioned for cyber-enabled fraud, money laundering, and human trafficking. Additionally, a Malaysian individual involved in defrauding U.S. victims through Africa-based scam networks was sanctioned.

In a parallel action, OFAC issued a Cuba-related Determination pursuant to Executive Order 14404, targeting the electronics, manufacturing, marine, and technology sectors of the Cuban economy. This determination paves the way for sanctions against any foreign person operating in these sectors.

The Cuba designations also included eight entities and two individuals associated with the Cuban regime's oil shipping networks, state-owned import and technical-support entities, and China-based suppliers to the Cuban military. Five vessels were identified as blocked property, including the EMILIA, GLORIA C, MARIA CRISTINA, ESPERANZA, and LOURDES, further restricting Cuba's energy and maritime resources.

articles.headline: OFAC Sanctions India-Based Maritime Network for Facilitating Iranian Oil Shipments, Issues Alert
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) imposed new Iran-related designations on an India-based maritime network accused of facilitating Iranian oil shipments through fraudulent vessel registrations and certifications. The sanctions target Suniel Kumar Sharma, his wife Jaspreet Preeti Shahid, two other Indian nationals, and nine associated entities.

According to the Treasury, this network established unauthorized ship registries and maritime classification services, enabling sanctioned tankers transporting Iranian petroleum to operate under false flags. Some of these vessels reportedly supported Iran's military and its proxies.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC published an Iran-related Alert titled 'Iranian Shadow Fleet Reliance on False Flags for Sanctions Evasion.' This alert warns maritime operators about the significant risks of designation or penalties for providing services to vessels using false flags to circumvent U.S. sanctions on Iran.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Oil & Gas Journal

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-related General License for PdVSA 2020 8.5 Percent Bond
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Venezuela-related General License 5AA, which further delays the effectiveness of the authorization in GL 5 until December 18, 2026. This general license pertains to certain transactions related to the Petróleos de Venezuela, S.A. (PdVSA) 2020 8.5 Percent Bond.

Between October 24, 2019, and December 18, 2026, there is no authorization in effect that licenses against subsection 1(a)(iii) of Executive Order 13835 applicable to the holders of the PdVSA 2020 8.5 percent bond. Consequently, transactions related to the sale or transfer of CITGO shares in connection with this bond remain prohibited unless specifically authorized by OFAC.
OFAC also issued one amended Frequently Asked Question, FAQ 595, providing further clarification on the implications of this general license and the ongoing prohibitions.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-related General License for International Development Bank
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued Iran General License FF-1, authorizing the wind down of transactions involving the International Development Bank for Investment and Finance, also known as Iraq Development Bank. This amended general license is effective immediately.

General License FF-1 replaces and supersedes the previous Iran General License FF. It specifically authorizes transactions ordinarily incident and necessary to wind down activities with the designated bank and certain majority-owned entities through December 1, 2026.

The issuance of this amended general license requires that any payments to blocked persons must be made into blocked accounts located in the United States, ensuring continued compliance with sanctions regulations during the wind-down period.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.headline: OFAC Sanctions North Korean IT Worker Schemes and DRC-Related Entities
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting North Korean government-run IT worker schemes. These schemes are accused of defrauding U.S. businesses and generating revenue for North Korea's illicit weapons programs through the use of fraudulent identities and other deceptive tactics to secure employment.

In a separate action, OFAC also imposed designations related to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). These designations target entities and individuals for facilitating Rwanda's support for the March 23 Movement (M23) and its political wing in eastern DRC.

The Treasury Department stated that these actions aim to hold Rwanda accountable under the Washington Accords and pressure the country to cease its support for M23 and withdraw its forces from eastern DRC.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.headline: Extreme Networks Settles with OFAC for $1.53 Million Over Russia Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc., resolving potential civil liability for nine apparent violations of Russia-related sanctions. The settlement amount is $1,529,685.

The apparent violations involved the export of networking equipment and services to a blocked Russian defense manufacturer. OFAC determined that these violations were voluntarily self-disclosed by Extreme Networks and were considered egregious.

This enforcement action highlights OFAC's continued focus on preventing U.S. companies from engaging in transactions that directly or indirectly benefit sanctioned entities, particularly those in the defense sector of adversarial nations.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Filing Reports
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) regarding blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC. These updates aim to provide clearer guidance to U.S. persons and financial institutions on their compliance obligations under OFAC regulations.

The amendments address various aspects of reporting requirements, including the types of transactions that must be reported, the timing for filing reports, and the information required in such submissions. This is part of OFAC's ongoing effort to enhance transparency and efficiency in sanctions compliance.

These updated FAQs serve as a critical resource for entities navigating the complexities of sanctions compliance, offering practical insights to ensure adherence to U.S. sanctions laws and avoid potential penalties.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related Entities, Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations as part of its ongoing efforts to counter the Iranian regime's illicit activities. These designations target individuals and entities involved in various sectors supporting the Iranian economy and its destabilizing actions.

In a separate but related action, OFAC also announced the removal of certain Belarus and North Korea designations from its Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List. Specifically, Chinese national Lu Hezheng and two Chinese entities (Shanghai Moxing Cultural Media Co. Ltd. and Shanghai Hongman Cartoon and Animation Design Studio) were delisted from the North Korea sanctions program.

Additionally, Belarusian national Andrei Alekseevich Rybakov was removed from the Belarus sanctions program. OFAC also issued new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses and amended several Frequently Asked Questions to provide updated guidance.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Export Compliance Daily

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes PAIPA Designations on Chinese Entities, Issues Associated General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA), targeting several Chinese entities. These designations aim to counter threats to American intellectual property and national security.

Among the entities added to OFAC's Non-SDN Menu Based Sanctions List (NS-MBS List) are Beijing Qiji Chuangtan Phase I Venture Capital Center Limited Partnership (also known as Miracle Plus RMB Fund I), Beijing Qiji Chuangtan Phase II Venture Capital Center Limited Partnership (also known as Miracle Plus RMB Fund II), and Qiji Chuangtan Beijing Investment Management Co Ltd (also known as Miracleplus).

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued two associated General Licenses: PAIPA General License 1, 'Transactions Authorized Pursuant to the Cyber-Related Sanctions Regulations,' and PAIPA General License 2, 'Authorizing the Wind Down of Transactions Involving Certain Entities Blocked on October 19, 2026.' General License 2 provides a wind-down period through January 19, 2027.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Venezuela-related General License for Earthquake Relief
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued Venezuela-related General License 60A, 'Authorizing Transactions Related to Earthquake Relief Efforts in Venezuela.' This new general license aims to facilitate humanitarian aid and recovery efforts in the country.

General License 60A authorizes transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under the Venezuela Sanctions Regulations, specifically those ordinarily incident and necessary to provide earthquake relief. This action underscores the U.S. commitment to supporting humanitarian efforts in Venezuela.
In addition to the general license, OFAC also issued one amended Frequently Asked Question, FAQ 1263, to provide further guidance and clarification on the scope and application of this authorization.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related Individuals and Entities, Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations, adding 16 individuals and 10 entities to its Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List. These designations are part of Operation Economic Outcast, targeting Iran's international financial networks and shadow banking architecture.

Among the designated entities are International Development Bank for Investment and Finance (also known as Iraq Development Bank), Chabahar International Bank Overseas Company, and Jazireh International Bank Company, along with several exchange companies including Abolhasan Jalali and Partners Exchange Company and Bavi and Partners Exchange Company.

OFAC also issued new and amended General Licenses, including Iran-related General License FF, authorizing the wind down of transactions involving International Development Bank for Investment and Finance. Additionally, a new Cuba-related FAQ (FAQ 1276) and an amended Russia-related FAQ (FAQ 1225) were issued.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cuban State-Owned Bank, Issues New Cuba-Related FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a new Cuba designation, targeting Banco Internacional de Comercio S.A. (BICSA), a Cuban state-owned bank. This designation was made pursuant to Executive Order 14404 for providing services to Iran-based Karafarin Bank, which was sanctioned by Treasury in 2020.
This action underscores the U.S. government's continued pressure on the Cuban regime and its financial facilitators, particularly those with ties to sanctioned entities in other adversarial nations.

In conjunction with this designation, OFAC issued a new Cuba-related Frequently Asked Question (FAQ 1276), providing further guidance and clarification on the implications of this action for U.S. persons and financial institutions.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Pays $1,529,685 to Settle OFAC Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc. has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of U.S. sanctions. The settlement addresses nine apparent violations related to the export of networking equipment and services to a blocked Russian defense manufacturer.

OFAC determined that the apparent violations were voluntarily self-disclosed by Extreme Networks and were considered egregious. This settlement highlights the importance of robust compliance programs, especially for companies operating in sectors with high sanctions risk.

The enforcement action serves as a reminder to U.S. companies of their obligations to ensure that their products and services do not directly or indirectly benefit sanctioned entities or contribute to activities prohibited by U.S. sanctions programs.

articles.headline: Bank of America, N.A. Assessed $11,662,930 Penalty by OFAC
body: Bank of America, N.A. has been assessed a civil monetary penalty of $11,662,930 by the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). The penalty addresses apparent violations of various U.S. sanctions programs.

Details of the specific violations leading to this significant penalty were outlined in OFAC's enforcement release. This action underscores OFAC's commitment to holding financial institutions accountable for lapses in sanctions compliance.

The substantial fine serves as a strong deterrent and emphasizes the critical need for comprehensive and effective sanctions compliance controls within large financial institutions to prevent illicit transactions.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Pays $175,015 for OFAC Sanctions Violations
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics has agreed to pay $175,015 to the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of U.S. sanctions. The settlement pertains to transactions involving a designated entity.

The apparent violations involved Pegasus coordinating the purchase and shipment of a customized sugar packet-filling machine from a designated entity, Youli, which had changed its name to Huizhou Youli Fushi Co., Ltd. after its designation.

This enforcement action highlights the importance for logistics companies to conduct thorough due diligence on all parties involved in a transaction, including suppliers and their affiliates, to ensure compliance with sanctions regulations.

The details of the violations were not immediately made public but typically involve unauthorized transactions with sanctioned persons or entities.

This significant penalty against an individual underscores OFAC's commitment to enforcing sanctions across all types of actors, not just corporations. It serves as a reminder that individuals can face substantial financial consequences for non-compliance.
The enforcement action emphasizes the need for all U.S. persons to understand and adhere to OFAC regulations, particularly when engaging in international financial or commercial activities.

This penalty serves as a reminder that all U.S. persons and entities are responsible for understanding and complying with OFAC regulations to prevent unauthorized transactions with sanctioned countries, entities, or individuals.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
